title: A Radiators for the Undertow
premise: Emrys Pemberton, a piano tuner who reads a house's history through its radiators, has spent five years keeping her family's secrets by never quite finishing her sentences. At her mother's funeral, a stranger greets the mourners with a surname nobody in the family uses, cracking open the question of who her mother really was and who Emrys has been pretending to be. Returning to the decaying family house in Cornwall, she follows the heat and hum of its old radiators through rooms of buried memory, uncovering a second family, a changed name, and the truth of the night her brother disappeared. In the end, Emrys chooses truth over loyalty—speaking the whole story aloud at last, losing her invisibility but finally gaining herself.
about_author: K. M. Vasquez is a former architectural conservator who spent a decade restoring historic houses and listening to what they kept. She writes literary fiction about families, buildings, and the stories both refuse to let go of.

chapters.title: The Pitch of Rooms
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. At her mother's funeral, Emrys performs the role of the quiet, competent daughter she has perfected, tuning the church piano to steady herself. When a grey-eyed stranger offers condolences using a surname no one recognizes, her rehearsed composure fractures. The emotional beat is the first hairline crack: grief tangled with the sudden vertigo of not knowing her own family.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV, with flashbacks. Back in her flat above the tuning shop, Emrys catalogs the family's unwritten rules—topics approached and abandoned mid-sentence for five years. Her brother Daniel's absence is the room no one enters. The beat is claustrophobic tenderness: love maintained through silence, and the growing suspicion that the silence was never mutual.

chapters.title: The Stranger at the Gate
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. The grey-eyed stranger, a woman named Ilsa, appears at the shop and leaves a brass radiator valve and a note: 'She kept our name too.' Emrys, rattled, decides to return to the derelict family house in Cornwall rather than let a stranger own the story. The beat is reluctant resolve—curiosity finally outweighing the comfort of not knowing.

chapters.title: What the Pipes Remember
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. In the cold house, Emrys reads its history through the radiators: a nursery warmed for a child she never knew existed, a room re-plumbed to hide something. She finds a child's initials scratched beneath the nursery wallpaper. The beat is eerie wonder turning to dread as the house confirms Ilsa wasn't lying.

chapters.title: Letters in the Boiler Room
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Behind the boiler she discovers a tin of letters in her mother's handwriting, addressed to someone called 'Nell'—apologetic, evasive, increasingly desperate over two decades. The letters reveal her mother lived under another name before marriage. The beat is betrayal's first full ache: the mother she mourned was partly a construction.

chapters.title: Ilsa's Version
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Ilsa, Nell's daughter, recounts her childhood: the woman called 'Aunt Vera' who visited each autumn, the gifts, the abrupt ending. She believes Emrys's mother was her real mother's sister—or more. The beat is the destabilizing experience of hearing your mother described as a stranger, and recognizing grief in a mirror.

chapters.title: The Night the Heat Failed
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV, deep flashback structure. Piecing together radiator service records and a neighbor's recollection, Emrys reconstructs the winter of 1989: the boiler failure, the argument overheard through pipes, and the night her brother Daniel walked out after learning the truth—and never came back. The beat is horrified comprehension; her family's silence has a body count of sorts.

chapters.title: Daniel's Address
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Following a return address in the letters' last envelope, Emrys finds Daniel living under a changed name two counties away, alive, unremarkable, and furious to be found. He refuses to come home but confirms everything, and tells her their mother begged him to stay silent 'for Nell's sake.' The beat is bitter relief—truth obtained, but at the cost of the last comfortable lie.

chapters.title: Bleeding the Radiators
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV, climax. At a gathering of both families at the house, with Ilsa present, Emrys does what she has never done: she says the whole thing, start to finish, no trailing off. The room erupts—accusations, denials, Ilsa weeping, Daniel arriving unbidden at the door. The beat is the terrifying liberation of a sentence finally finished.

chapters.title: A House That Holds Warmth
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV, resolution. Months later, Emrys restores the house's heating and, with it, something of herself; Ilsa visits as what she now is—family of a complicated kind—and Daniel writes twice a year. Emrys keeps tuning pianos but no longer tunes her sentences down. The beat is quiet, earned peace: identity not as inheritance but as choice.
